```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

# Everything the post shows comes from the analysis repository
base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference/main/"

key   <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/key_numbers.csv"))
cov   <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/coverage.csv"))
small <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/small_sample.csv"))
nulls <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/null_summary.csv"))
pw    <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/power.csv"))
wsum  <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/widget_summary.csv"))
wpow  <- read_csv(paste0(base, "results/widget_power.csv"))

ks <- function(stat) key$value[key$stat == stat]
ns <- function(stat) nulls$value[nulls$stat == stat]
num <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
pct <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), 100 * x)
pctabs <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), 100 * abs(x))

cov_at <- function(n, level) {
  cov$coverage[cov$n == n & cov$level == level]
}
small_at <- function(n, col) small[[col]][small$n_per_month == n]
power_at <- function(n, delta) {
  d <- pw[pw$n == n, ]
  d$power[which.min(abs(d$delta - delta))]
}
```

Every month the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes an unemployment rate, and
every month the news reports how it moved. The number is treated as a fact
about the economy. It is not: it is an estimate from a sample of roughly
100,000 people, and a different sample of the same size would have produced a
slightly different number. How much does that matter? This post answers it by
simulation: how precise the rate is, whether the interval we publish really
contains the truth, and what a smaller survey would have concluded.

The data are the IPUMS Current Population Survey basic monthly microdata,
January 2019 to August 2026. I compare **January 2019** with **January 2024**
— the same month in different years, so the labour market's seasonal pattern
cancels out — and ask whether the unemployment rate really changed. It was
`r pct(ks("rate_2019"))`% in January 2019
(`r format(ks("n_2019"), big.mark = ",")` people) and
`r pct(ks("rate_2024"))`% in January 2024
(`r format(ks("n_2024"), big.mark = ",")` people): a fall of
`r pctabs(ks("diff"))` percentage points. Is that a change in the economy,
or a change in who answered the phone?

## 1. Build the interval by resampling

The usual way to put an interval around an estimate is a formula that assumes
the sample was drawn at random from a population of equal-weight people. The
CPS is neither simple nor equal-weighted — its final person weights run from
177 to 13,140 — so we resample instead: draw the same number of interviewed
people at random *with replacement*, recompute the weighted rate, and repeat
2,000 times. The spread of those 2,000 numbers is the bootstrap distribution:
how much the estimate would have moved if we had interviewed somebody else.

![Bootstrap distributions of the January 2024 rate and of the change from January 2019.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference/main/results/fig1_bootstrap.png)

The bootstrap interval for January 2024 is `r pct(ks("ci_low_2024"))`% to
`r pct(ks("ci_high_2024"))`%, and for the change between the two months
`r pct(ks("ci_low_diff"))` to `r pct(ks("ci_high_diff"))` percentage points.
The textbook interval for the same change is `r pct(ks("wald_low_diff"))` to
`r pct(ks("wald_high_diff"))` — 49% narrower. That gap is a design effect: the
textbook formula understates the real sampling error of the CPS by almost
half, so every interval built that way is too narrow.

## 2. Does a 95% interval contain the truth 95% of the time?

An interval is a promise about how often it will contain the truth, and
promises should be checked: build a population with a known unemployment rate,
sample it over and over, and count how often the interval contains the
truth.

![Simulated coverage of the interval, and coverage on the real CPS data.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference/main/results/fig2_coverage.png)

The promise is kept: at 95%, coverage is `r pct(cov_at(250, 0.95), 1)`% with
250 interviews and `r pct(cov_at(80923, 0.95), 1)`% with 80,923, and every
other nominal level lands within about a point of what it promised.

The same test on the real CPS data is less comfortable. Repeating the
experiment 1,000 times with smaller surveys, the bootstrap interval contains
the full-sample estimate about `r round(100 * mean(small$coverage_boot))`% of
the time; the textbook interval about
`r round(100 * mean(small$coverage_wald))`% of the time. The bootstrap is at
least honest about a weighted proportion being a lopsided statistic. The
formula is not.

## 3. A p-value is an area under a simulated null distribution

To say "the rate changed", we test H0: the two months have the same rate.
Under H0 the estimated change is still random, with a distribution centred on
zero. Simulating that experiment 20,000 times gives the null distribution
below; everything outside ±`r pctabs(ns("crit_low"))` points is the
rejection region, 5% of the null distribution by construction.

![The simulated null distribution of the estimated change, with the rejection region and the observed change.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference/main/results/fig3_null.png)

The observed change of `r pct(ks("diff"))` points falls just inside that
region, and the p-value is simply the area of the null distribution beyond
what we observed: `r num(ns("p_sim"), 3)`. The textbook formula, using the
too-small standard error, would have said
`r format(ns("p_norm"), scientific = FALSE, digits = 2)`. Both are correct
arithmetic; only one is honest about how much the estimate can move.

## 4. How much could this survey have found?

The most useful thing a simulation tells you is what a survey *could* have
found. The power to detect the change we measured rises from
`r pct(power_at(1000, ks("diff")), 1)`% with 1,000 interviews per month to
`r pct(power_at(80923, ks("diff")), 1)`% with 80,923.

![Power curves: the chance of detecting a real change at different sample sizes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference/main/results/fig4_power.png)

The interactive figure below puts that in your hands: drag the slider to change
how many people were interviewed each month, and watch the statistic move, the
p-value fall, and the verdict flip. It assumes the two months are the same size,
so at the top of the slider it reads a p-value of 0.019, slightly above the
0.016 that the two real months (97,181 and 80,923 people) gave.

```{r}
#| label: interactive-power
#| fig-height: 7.2

z_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)
crit_z <- 1.96

xl <- seq(-4, -crit_z, length.out = 120)
xr <- seq(4, crit_z, length.out = 120)
left_x  <- c(xl, -crit_z, -4);  left_y  <- c(dnorm(xl), 0, 0)
right_x <- c(xr, crit_z, 4);   right_y <- c(dnorm(xr), 0, 0)

power_grid <- sort(unique(wpow$delta)) * 100          # percentage points
power_y <- lapply(wsum$n, function(n) {
  p <- wpow$power[wpow$n == n]
  approx(sort(unique(wpow$delta)) * 100, p, xout = power_grid)$y
})

label_for <- function(i) {
  sprintf("n = %s per month<br>z = %+.2f &nbsp;|&nbsp; p-value = %s<br>%s",
          format(wsum$n[i], big.mark = ","), wsum$z_obs[i],
          ifelse(wsum$p_value[i] < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", wsum$p_value[i])),
          ifelse(wsum$p_value[i] < 0.05,
                 "reject H0: the rate really changed",
                 "cannot reject H0: not enough evidence"))
}

p <- plot_ly()

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = z_grid, y = dnorm(z_grid), type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
  line = list(color = "#1f77b4", width = 2), fill = "tozeroy",
  fillcolor = "rgba(31,119,180,0.18)", hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE,
  xaxis = "x", yaxis = "y")

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = left_x, y = left_y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", fill = "toself",
  fillcolor = "rgba(214,39,40,0.18)", line = list(width = 0), hoverinfo = "skip",
  showlegend = FALSE, xaxis = "x", yaxis = "y")

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = right_x, y = right_y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", fill = "toself",
  fillcolor = "rgba(214,39,40,0.18)", line = list(width = 0), hoverinfo = "skip",
  showlegend = FALSE, xaxis = "x", yaxis = "y")

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = c(wsum$z_obs[1], wsum$z_obs[1]), y = c(0, 0.42), type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines", line = list(color = "#222222", width = 2, dash = "dash"),
  hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, xaxis = "x", yaxis = "y")

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = power_grid, y = power_y[[1]], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
  line = list(color = "#f0a202", width = 2.5), hoverinfo = "skip",
  showlegend = FALSE, xaxis = "x2", yaxis = "y2")

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = c(ks("diff") * 100, ks("diff") * 100), y = c(0, 1), type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines", line = list(color = "#222222", width = 1.2, dash = "dash"),
  hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, xaxis = "x2", yaxis = "y2")

p <- p |> add_trace(
  x = power_grid, y = rep(0.8, length(power_grid)), type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines", line = list(color = "#8c8c8c", width = 1, dash = "dot"),
  hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE, xaxis = "x2", yaxis = "y2")

steps <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(wsum)), function(i) {
  list(
    label = paste0(format(wsum$n[i], big.mark = ","), " per month"),
    method = "update",
    args = list(
      list(x = list(c(wsum$z_obs[i], wsum$z_obs[i]), power_grid),
           y = list(c(0, 0.42), power_y[[i]])),
      list("annotations[0].text" = label_for(i)),
      c(3, 4)
    )
  )
})

p <- p |> layout(
  xaxis  = list(domain = c(0, 1), anchor = "y", range = c(-4, 4),
                title = "Test statistic z", zeroline = FALSE, title_font = list(size = 11)),
  yaxis  = list(domain = c(0.60, 1), anchor = "x", range = c(0, 0.52),
                title = "Null density", title_font = list(size = 11)),
  xaxis2 = list(domain = c(0, 1), anchor = "y2",
                title = "True change in the unemployment rate (percentage points)",
                title_font = list(size = 11)),
  yaxis2 = list(domain = c(0.19, 0.45), anchor = "x2", range = c(0, 1),
                title = "Power", title_font = list(size = 11)),
  title = list(text = paste0("How much evidence does the sample size buy?<br>",
                             "<sup>Drag the slider: the statistic moves, the ",
                             "p-value falls, and the verdict can flip</sup>"),
               font = list(size = 14), x = 0.02, xanchor = "left"),
  sliders = list(list(
    active = 0,
    currentvalue = list(prefix = "Sample size: "),
    pad = list(t = 30, b = 10),
    x = 0.13, y = 0.08, len = 0.80,
    steps = steps
  )),
  annotations = list(
    list(x = 0.1, y = 0.47, xref = "x", yref = "y", showarrow = FALSE,
         align = "center", text = label_for(1), font = list(size = 12, color = "#222222")),
    list(x = -3.55, y = 0.30, xref = "x", yref = "y", showarrow = FALSE,
         text = "null distribution under H0", font = list(size = 10, color = "#1f77b4"),
         xanchor = "left"),
    list(x = -2.9, y = 0.20, xref = "x", yref = "y", showarrow = FALSE,
         text = "rejection region (5%)", font = list(size = 10, color = "#d62728")),
    list(x = ks("diff") * 100 - 0.02, y = 0.62, xref = "x2", yref = "y2",
         showarrow = FALSE, text = "observed change", font = list(size = 10, color = "#222222"),
         xanchor = "right"),
    list(x = -0.78, y = 0.845, xref = "x2", yref = "y2", showarrow = FALSE,
         text = "80% power", font = list(size = 10, color = "#8c8c8c"), xanchor = "left")
  ),
  margin = list(l = 65, r = 30, t = 105, b = 55),
  hovermode = "closest"
)

# Print the widget as the last expression of the chunk (not as an assignment),
# otherwise knitr captures no output and the figure never reaches the page.
p |> config(displaylogo = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
```

A survey of 1,000 people a month would have missed this real change 94% of
the time and reported "no change". Even the full CPS sample has roughly a
one-in-three chance of missing a change this size. A p-value of
`r num(ns("p_sim"), 3)` is therefore not a statement that the change was
economically important — it is a statement that this sample could see it.

## Takeaway

A confidence interval and a p-value are statements about the data you
happened to collect, not about the world. The bootstrap says how much your
estimate would move if you collected slightly different data; simulation says
how often the interval you built would have been right; and the null
distribution turns "significant" into a tail area you can point at. None of
this replaces judgement, but it puts a number on the part of a conclusion
that came from luck.

The unemployment rate fell by `r pctabs(ks("diff"))` points between January
2019 and January 2024, and this sample is large enough to notice it: the 95%
interval runs from `r pct(ks("ci_low_diff"))` to
`r pct(ks("ci_high_diff"))` points, and the simulated p-value is
`r num(ns("p_sim"), 3)`. The same comparison in a survey a tenth the size
would have been indistinguishable from noise — and a confident headline would
have said nothing changed. Simulation is what tells the two apart.

*Code and data: [github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference](https://github.com/Peterjianghaowen/blog8-simulation-inference). Data source: IPUMS Current Population Survey, University of Minnesota.*
